prompt: tcpdump on the ISP's router printed the tunnel's packets as `proto ESP (…)`. What IP protocol number is ESP?
hint: AH is the next number up.

prompt: A partner insists on AH because it also protects the IP header. Their office sits behind a NAT router. What happens?
hint: What does NAT change, and what does AH cover?

choices.text: It works, because AH skips whatever NAT changes
choices.why: AH covers the addresses on purpose; that is exactly what breaks it.

choices.text: The NAT router refuses to forward protocol 51
choices.why: It forwards it; the failure shows up at the far end, in the check.

choices.text: Every packet fails its check at the far end
choices.why: Right. NAT rewrote an address the check value covered.

choices.text: It works as long as both sides use tunnel mode
choices.why: In tunnel mode the outer header is what NAT rewrites, and AH covers it.

prompt: With ESP in tunnel mode, what source address does the ISP's router read on a packet going from the laptop to the till?
hint: Which header is outside the encryption?

choices.why: The laptop's address is in the inner header, which is encrypted.
Right. The new outer header carries hq's public address.
That is branch, the destination of the outer packet.
hq's LAN address never appears on the ISP's side.

prompt: Match each thing ESP guarantees to the part of ESP that provides it.
hint: One part only selects the key.

pairs.left: Nobody on the path reads the payload
A recorded packet sent again is refused

prompt: Two Linux servers in one data centre must encrypt the database traffic between them, and nothing else. Which mode fits, and why?
hint: Who are the endpoints of the traffic?

choices.text: Tunnel mode, because only it encrypts the payload
choices.why: Both modes encrypt what follows the header they keep.

choices.text: Transport mode, because it hides their addresses from the switch
choices.why: Transport mode leaves the addresses readable.

choices.text: Tunnel mode, since transport mode cannot cross a switch
choices.why: A switch forwards frames whatever the mode inside them.

choices.text: Transport: the servers are the endpoints
choices.why: Right. No gateway is involved, so no second IP header is needed.

prompt: What does the pre-shared key in swanctl.conf do?
hint: The traffic keys come from somewhere else.

choices.text: Encrypts the traffic between the two networks
choices.why: The traffic keys come from the Diffie-Hellman exchange, fresh each time.

choices.text: Proves to each router who the other one is
choices.why: Right. It is used for the proof in IKE_AUTH and for nothing else.

choices.text: Decides which algorithms the two sides use
choices.why: That is what `proposals` and `esp_proposals` do.

choices.text: Encrypts the IKE messages, but not the traffic
choices.why: IKE_AUTH is encrypted with keys from the Diffie-Hellman exchange too.

prompt: With `start_action = trap`, the laptop's first ping to the till was lost and the next two came back. Why?
hint: It happened again after the connection was torn down.

choices.text: The till's router was still learning the laptop's MAC
choices.why: Address resolution does not lose a ping; the loss followed the tunnel starting, both times.

choices.text: It set the negotiation off and was dropped while it ran
choices.why: Right. There were no keys yet to protect it with.

choices.text: The first ESP packet of an SA always fails its ICV
choices.why: It never became ESP at all; there was no SA yet.

choices.text: The capture on the ISP's router held it back
choices.why: A capture copies packets; it never stops one.

prompt: Which of these can the ISP read in the IKE exchange between hq and branch?
hint: Which exchange goes in clear?

choices.text: The names hq.example.com and branch.example.com
choices.why: The identities travel in IKE_AUTH, which is encrypted.

choices.text: A hash of the pre-shared key
choices.why: The key never crosses, and the proof made with it is in the encrypted exchange.

choices.text: The algorithms each side offered
choices.why: Right. IKE_SA_INIT is in clear, offers and all.

choices.text: The two networks the tunnel will join
choices.why: The traffic selectors are in IKE_AUTH, encrypted.

prompt: Put the start of the tunnel in order, from the laptop's first ping.
hint: Nothing can be encrypted before there is a secret.
items: The laptop's ping falls into the trap
IKE_SA_INIT goes out and comes back, in clear
Both routers compute the same secret
IKE_AUTH goes out and comes back, encrypted
trap: The secret comes from the first exchange's public values, so IKE_AUTH cannot be encrypted before it.

prompt: With no NAT in the way and MOBIKE off, all four IKE messages between the offices used UDP port ___.
hint: The port tcpdump filtered on first.

prompt: The laptop's ping was 84 bytes inside the tunnel and 140 on the wire. How many bytes did IPsec add?
hint: The new IP header is part of it.

prompt: hq's listing shows `out 41b696e1`. Which packets carry `spi=0x41b696e1` on the wire?
hint: An SA is one direction.

choices.text: Those branch sends to hq
choices.why: Those carry 7fdf3ac6, hq's `in`.

choices.text: The IKE messages, in both directions
choices.why: The IKE SA has its own 64-bit SPIs.

choices.text: Every ESP packet of the tunnel, both ways
choices.why: Each direction has its own SA and its own SPI.

choices.text: Only those hq sends to branch
choices.why: Right. The reply in the capture carried 0x7fdf3ac6.

prompt: Both counters of the CHILD SA said 168 bytes for 2 packets, while the ISP saw ESP packets of 140 bytes. Why do the two not agree?
hint: Divide 168 by 2.

choices.text: The SA counts the packets before encryption
choices.why: Right. 168 / 2 = 84, the laptop's ping as it sent it.

choices.text: tcpdump on the ISP counted the Ethernet header too
choices.why: 140 is the IP length, and 2 × 140 would be 280 anyway.

choices.text: One of the two pings was lost between the routers
choices.why: Two packets were counted, 84 bytes each.

choices.text: AES-GCM compresses the payload before sending it
choices.why: Encryption compresses nothing; the wire packet is the larger one.

prompt: With ESP in tunnel mode between the offices, what can the ISP still learn?
hint: What is outside the encryption?

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: The outer header, the SPI and the sizes are all readable.

choices.text: Which machines inside the offices are talking
choices.why: The inner addresses are encrypted.

choices.text: That the offices talk, when, and how much
choices.why: Right. Encryption hides contents, not the fact of the conversation.

choices.text: The URLs requested, but not the pages
choices.why: grep found GET in none of the ten packets.

prompt: The CHILD SA said `rekeying in 3288s, expires in 3957s`. What happens at the rekey?
hint: It comes before the expiry for a reason.

choices.text: The tunnel goes down until IKE runs again
choices.why: Rekeying before the expiry exists precisely so it does not.

choices.text: The pre-shared key is replaced by a new one
choices.why: The pre-shared key is configured; only the traffic keys change.

choices.text: New keys are made while the old ones still work
choices.why: Right. Traffic never waits for a negotiation after the first.

choices.text: The sequence number goes back to zero, nothing else
choices.why: A new SA comes with new keys and new SPIs, not just a new count.

prompt: A log shows `selected proposal: IKE:…` and then ends with `received AUTHENTICATION_FAILED notify error`. What does that rule out?
hint: Which step succeeded?

choices.text: A wrong pre-shared key on one side
choices.why: That is one of the causes of exactly this message.

choices.text: That the two sides share no algorithm
choices.why: Right. A proposal was selected in IKE_SA_INIT, so they agreed on algorithms.

choices.text: A wrong id configured for the peer
choices.why: A wrong id ends in the same notification.

choices.text: Nothing; every mistake ends this way
choices.why: Different networks end in TS_UNACCEPTABLE, and no common algorithm in NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN.

prompt: A partner's router has your side as 10.50.0.0/16, while yours offers 10.50.1.0/24 and 172.20.0.0/24. The IKE SA comes up, and the CHILD SA fails with TS_UNACCEPTABLE. What do you change first?
hint: Which step failed, and what is decided there?

choices.text: The pre-shared key, on both routers
choices.why: Authentication succeeded; the IKE SA is up.

choices.text: Both routers to AH, which has no selectors
choices.why: AH has selectors like ESP, and no NAT-friendliness.

choices.text: Make the two sides' selectors mirror each other
choices.why: Right. 172.20.0.0/24 is in no network the partner allows, and nothing narrows it into one.

choices.text: Open UDP 4500 on the partner's firewall
choices.why: IKE got through fine; this is about which networks the tunnel joins.

prompt: Match each line in the initiator's log to its most likely cause.
hint: Each is refused at a different step.

prompt: tshark showed the first IKE_SA_INIT as a 506-byte frame, and strongSwan logged the same message as 464 bytes. How many bytes of headers wrap each IKE message on that link?
hint: Ethernet, IP and UDP.

prompt: Why did the laptop's tunnel move to UDP port 4500?
hint: What does the home router need in order to share one address?

choices.text: Port 500 is reserved for site-to-site tunnels
choices.why: Port 500 is IKE's, for any tunnel; the laptop started on it.

choices.text: ESP needs a port number in order to be encrypted
choices.why: Encryption has nothing to do with ports; the offices' ESP had none.

choices.text: ESP has no ports for the NAT to tell it apart by
choices.why: Right. Inside UDP it has ports like any other conversation.

choices.text: The office's firewall blocks protocol 50
choices.why: The offices' own tunnel used protocol 50 through the same router.

prompt: Why does hq give the home laptop 10.30.0.1 rather than letting it use 192.168.1.50 inside the tunnel?
hint: How many homes use 192.168.1.0/24?

choices.text: Private addresses are not allowed inside ESP
choices.why: The offices' own tunnel carried 192.168 addresses.

choices.text: The virtual address hides the laptop from the ISP
choices.why: The ISP sees 198.51.100.77 either way, and the inside is encrypted anyway.

choices.text: The home router would rewrite 192.168.1.50 inside the tunnel
choices.why: A NAT cannot see inside ESP at all.

choices.text: Thousands of homes use it; the office could not route it back
choices.why: Right. An address the office hands out is one it knows how to reach.

prompt: Which of these did the capture on the ISP's router show for the laptop at home? Choose all that apply.
hint: The ISP is on the far side of the home router.

choices.text: IKE_SA_INIT on port 500
IKE_AUTH on port 4500, marked NONESP-encap
choices.why: Right: the second exchange had already moved.

choices.text: The laptop's home address, 192.168.1.50
choices.why: The home router rewrote it; only remote's own log shows it.

choices.text: ESP inside UDP, with its SPI readable
choices.why: Right: `UDP-encap: ESP(spi=0x0d6d6c89,seq=0x1)`.

choices.text: ESP as bare protocol 50, with no UDP
choices.why: That was the offices' tunnel; behind a NAT every packet was UDP.

prompt: Fifty staff connect from home with one shared pre-shared key. One of them leaves on bad terms. Which change removes the problem rather than today's symptom?
hint: The next person will leave too.

choices.text: Change the key and send it to the other forty-nine
choices.why: It fixes today and repeats the problem with the next departure.

choices.text: A certificate or login per person, each revocable alone
choices.why: Right. Removing one person then touches nobody else.

choices.text: Move the connections from port 500 to 4500
choices.why: The port has nothing to do with who holds the key.

choices.text: Switch the ESP proposal to a longer key
choices.why: The traffic keys were never the leak; the shared secret is.

prompt: A new branch sits behind its carrier's NAT. Its IKE_SA_INIT gets an answer, then IKE_AUTH is retransmitted until it times out. Tunnels between offices without NAT work. What fits best?
hint: Where does IKE_AUTH travel when a NAT is detected?

choices.text: The pre-shared key differs between the two sides
choices.why: A wrong key gets an answer, AUTH_FAILED, not silence.

choices.text: The traffic selectors do not mirror each other
choices.why: That fails after a successful IKE_AUTH, with TS_UNACCEPTABLE.

choices.text: Something on the path drops UDP 4500
choices.why: Right. Port 500 worked; after the NAT was detected IKE moved to 4500, and nothing came back from there.

choices.text: The two sides have no algorithm in common
choices.why: IKE_SA_INIT was answered, so a proposal was chosen.
